newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Aleman win confirmed in Nicaragua, Ortega cries foul.
newsitem.headline: Aleman win confirmed in Nicaragua, Ortega cries foul.

text.p: Sandinista leader Daniel Ortega vowed on Saturday that he would not recognise the legitimacy of President-elect Arnoldo Aleman's government despite official confirmation of his victory in the Oct. 20 elections.

His comments came after Nicaragua's Supreme Electoral Council rejected on Friday a Sandinista appeal for new voting in the departments of Managua and Matagalpa because of alleged fraud, ending more than a month of post-vote squabbling.
"It is the new government. It is a reality. But there is no consensus. There is no legitimacy," Ortega, who led Nicaragua's 1979-1990 left-wing Sandinista government, told reporters.
Aleman defeated Ortega by 51 percent to 37.7 percent in provisional results released by the council two weeks ago.
But Ortega refused to concede defeat and said he would recognise the legality but not the legitimacy of his government.
The head of the Organisation of American States (OAS), Cesar Gaviria, also issued a news release on Saturday endorsing the vote results as valid.
Ortega, for his part, continued on Saturday to maintain the vote was fraudulent.
"These elections did not fill the requirements demanded by law. This has degenerated into a crisis of confidence, a crisis of legitimacy, and this crisis could deepen," he said.
The Sandinista-owned newsapaper Barricada on Saturday led with the headline: "Fraud confirmed. Poor Nicaragua!"
Ortega said his party on Tuesday would present a proposal to stabilise the country, seeking a national understanding among the social and economic sectors.

At Aleman's jubilant Liberal Alliance headquarters in Managua, however, the portly right-wing president-elect extended an olive branch to the Sandinistas offering to work with them after he takes office on Jan. 10.

"Here, today, I make a call to Comandante Daniel Ortega that for the sake of Nicaragua we work together to make the transformations so that the dispossessed classes no longer must bear the suffering and poverty," Aleman told a news conference.

Analysts said if Aleman was to govern effectively he must reach an agreement with his left-wing rivals, the Sandinistas, who despite losing the presidency won almost 40 percent of the seats in the National Assembly, 51 city councils and remain a major force in the unions, army and police.

The Liberal Alliance won 42 of the 93 seats in Nicaragua's powerful National Assembly. The Sandinistas won 36, followed by a jumble of smaller parties with the remaining 15. The Liberals will need 48 votes to pass legislation.
